title: Genesis 12. The Cup of Calling.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 12. The Cup of Calling.
God speaks to a man with a barren wife in a city where his brother died.
Go from your country, your kindred, your father's house,
to the land I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation.
I will bless you.
I will make your name great.
You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you,
and him who curses you I will curse.
And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
The Cup of calling.
Not earned.
Not sought.
Not built.
God chooses a man who has nothing, no land, no children,
no future, and pours everything into him.
The man whose wife is barren is promised a nation.
The man whose father stopped short of Canaan is told to finish the journey.
The man with no name in the scattering at Babel is told:
I will make your name great.
The exact thing Babel tried to do by building,
make a name for themselves, God now does by calling.
The tower that could not reach heaven is replaced by a voice that comes down from heaven and finds one man.
Abram goes.
He is seventy-five years old.
He takes Sarai, Lot, everything they own,
and the people they acquired in Haran.
They set out for the land of Canaan.
They enter it.
Abram passes through the land to Shechem, to the oak of Moreh.
The Canaanites are in the land,
the people whose ancestor was cursed in chapter nine are living in the land God has just promised to Abram.
The promise is given inside occupied territory.
The Cup is handed to a man who does not hold the ground it rests on.
The Lord appears to Abram and says:
To your offspring I will give this land.
Not to Abram.
To his offspring.
The man whose wife is barren is told his children will inherit.
The promise reaches past the man who received it toward a generation that does not yet exist.
Abram builds an altar.
The first altar since Noah's, the one built after the flood.
The man who received a promise builds an altar to the God who spoke it.
Then he moves to the mountain east of Bethel, pitches his tent,
and builds another altar.
He calls on the name of the Lord.
The phrase from chapter four,
people began to call on the name of the Lord,
now becomes the practice of one man in a land that is not his.
He travels onward, still going toward the South.
Then famine comes.
The land God promised does not feed the man God called.
The ground that was cursed in chapter three,
that was drowned in chapter seven, that was promised in this chapter,
now it cannot sustain Abram.
He goes down to Egypt to sojourn there,
because the famine is severe.
As he approaches Egypt, he says to Sarai:
I know that you are a woman beautiful to look at.
When the Egyptians see you, they will say, This is his wife.
They will kill me, but they will let you live.
Say you are my sister,
that it may go well with me because of you,
and that my life may be spared for your sake.
The Cup that was just given, the covenant, the promise, the offspring,
the blessing of all nations,
is immediately endangered by the man who received it.
The vessel who heard God's voice gives away the wife through whom the promise must come.
The man who was told all families of the earth would be blessed through him hands the woman who carries that blessing to a foreign king to save his own life.
The Egyptians see Sarai.
She is very beautiful.
Pharaoh's princes praise her to Pharaoh.
She is taken into Pharaoh's house.
Abram is treated well for her sake.
He receives sheep, oxen, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys,
and camels.
The Cup of calling has become commerce.
The woman who carries the promise is traded for livestock.
The man who built altars accepts payment for his wife.
The vessel God filled is being emptied by the vessel itself.
But the Lord afflicts Pharaoh and his house with great plagues,
because of Sarai, Abram's wife.
God intervenes.
Not because Abram asked.
Not because Abram prayed.
Not because Abram built an altar or called on the name of the Lord.
God acts because the promise is at risk.
The Cup is preserved, not by Abram's faithfulness, but by God's.
The vessel that fumbled is held by the hand that filled it.
Pharaoh calls Abram: What is this you have done to me?
Why did you not tell me she was your wife?
Why did you say she is my sister,
so that I took her to be my wife?
Now then, here is your wife.
Take her and go.
The king of Egypt rebukes the man God called.
The man who heard the voice of God is corrected by a man who did not.
The vessel that was given the Cup is exposed by the one who unknowingly held its contents.
Pharaoh commands men concerning Abram,
and they send him away with his wife and all that he had.
This is the pattern that will repeat through all of Genesis:
God gives.
Man fumbles.
God preserves.
The Cup that was given in calling is carried out of Egypt,
not by the strength of the one who received it,
but by the faithfulness of the One who poured it.
The promise has not been fulfilled.
The land is not yet his.
The wife is still barren.
The offspring has not appeared.
But the vessel is moving, out of Egypt, back toward Canaan,
carrying a word that has not yet become flesh.
What began in a garden has narrowed to a man.
What was scattered across nations has been gathered into one family.
What was promised to all the earth has been placed in the hands of a man who just sold his wife for sheep.
The Cup holds.
Not because the vessel is strong.
Because the One who fills it does not let go.
